claims.text: In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm deploys resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (per kind_sorter.go in the Helm source).
Helm chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."
Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source (kind_sorter.go).

Helm's kind order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else.
A Helm chart can't express installing one subchart before another, or starting a Deployment after a Job completes.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with helm.sh/hook-weight annotations, and hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in Helm HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another or setting the dependsOn resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.
Pulumi's helm.v4.Chart supports the config.kubernetes.io/depends-on annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and dependsOn on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program is the most common adoption pattern.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with helm template and converting the YAML with pulumi convert --from kubernetes.
helm.v4.Chart renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
helm.v3.Release uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Pulumi installs a chart after the resources it depends on, resolving values at deploy time.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order with each resource ready before dependents, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and helm rollback restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and you roll forward by reverting program code and running pulumi up.
